description: Spot the sneaky thinking traps (cognitive distortions) that make life feel worse than it is — and learn how to reframe them.

1.definition: Seeing things as totally good or totally bad, with no middle. Life is usually somewhere in between.
1.scenarioDoneTo: You got a B on a spelling test and think, 'I'm a total failure at spelling.'
1.scenarioYouDo: You got a B on a spelling test and think, 'I'm a total failure at spelling.'

challenge.scenario: You got a B on a spelling test and think, 'I'm a total failure at spelling.' What's a truer thought?
options: 'A B means I got most of them right — I can practice the ones I missed.'
'Yeah, I'm the worst speller ever.'
'I should just stop trying at spelling.'

1.tip: Reframe: A B isn't 'failure' — it's mostly right. Look for the middle ground between 'perfect' and 'terrible.'

2.definition: Black-and-white thinking. If it's not perfect, it's a disaster. Real life almost always has shades of gray.
2.scenarioDoneTo: You missed one shot in the basketball game and think, 'I'm a terrible player, I should quit the team.'
2.scenarioYouDo: You missed one shot in the basketball game and think, 'I'm a terrible player, I should quit the team.'

challenge.scenario: You missed one shot and think, 'I should quit the team.' What's a healthier reframe?
options: 'One missed shot doesn't erase every shot I've made. Every player misses sometimes.'
'Yeah, one miss proves I don't belong.'
'I'll just never shoot again.'

2.tip: Reframe: 'One time doesn't equal always.' Look for evidence that shows the full picture, not just the worst moment.

3.definition: Dichotomous thinking treats outcomes as binary (success/failure, hero/villain) and ignores the nuance where most of life actually lives.
3.scenarioDoneTo: You didn't get accepted to your top-choice college and conclude your whole future is ruined.
3.scenarioYouDo: You didn't get accepted to your top-choice college and conclude your whole future is ruined.

challenge.scenario: You didn't get into your top-choice college and think, 'My future is over.' What's a more balanced reframe?
options: 'This one door closed, but I have real options. My future isn't decided by one school.'
'Yeah, that was my only path. It's all downhill from here.'
'I'll just not go to college at all now.'

3.tip: Reframe: Ask yourself, 'What's the gray area here?' Rarely is one event the whole story.

1.definition: Imagining the worst possible outcome, even when it's very unlikely.
1.scenarioDoneTo: Your friend didn't wave back at you and you think, 'They must hate me now, I'm going to lose all my friends.'
1.scenarioYouDo: Your friend didn't wave back at you and you think, 'They must hate me now, I'm going to lose all my friends.'

challenge.scenario: Your friend didn't wave back and you think, 'They hate me now.' What's a truer thought?
options: 'Maybe they didn't see me. I can just ask them later.'
'They definitely hate me forever.'
'I should stop being friends with them first.'

1.tip: Reframe: Ask, 'What's most likely?' Usually the boring explanation (they didn't see you) is the real one.

2.definition: Jumping to the worst-case scenario as if it's already happening. Your brain skips over all the more likely outcomes.
2.scenarioDoneTo: You have a small headache and immediately think, 'Something is seriously wrong with me.'
2.scenarioYouDo: You have a small headache and immediately think, 'Something is seriously wrong with me.'

challenge.scenario: You have a headache and jump straight to 'something's seriously wrong.' What's a healthier response?
options: 'Headaches usually mean I'm tired, thirsty, or stressed. Let me check those first.'
'I need to google every disease that causes headaches right now.'
'I should just panic and assume the worst.'

2.tip: Reframe: Rate the actual probability. 'What are the 5 most likely explanations?' The worst-case is almost never #1.

3.definition: Catastrophic thinking spins one negative signal into a doomsday chain (this bad thing → next bad thing → total collapse), often without evidence for any link in the chain.
3.scenarioDoneTo: Your boss schedules a 'quick chat' and you spiral: 'I'm getting fired → I can't pay rent → I'll be homeless.'
3.scenarioYouDo: Your boss schedules a 'quick chat' and you spiral: 'I'm getting fired → I can't pay rent → I'll be homeless.'

challenge.scenario: You spiral 'chat → fired → homeless' before the meeting even happens. What's a grounded reframe?
options: 'A quick chat could be a hundred things. I'll deal with what actually happens, not what I imagine.'
'I should update my resume and pack my things right now.'
'Assume the worst, that way I'm ready.'

3.tip: Reframe: Break the doom-chain. 'Even IF the worst happened, what would I actually do?' You're more resourceful than the spiral gives you credit for.

1.definition: Assuming you know what someone else is thinking — usually that it's something bad about you.
1.scenarioDoneTo: Your teacher looks at you and you think, 'She thinks I'm dumb.'
1.scenarioYouDo: Your teacher looks at you and you think, 'She thinks I'm dumb.'

challenge.scenario: You catch your teacher looking at you and think, 'She thinks I'm dumb.' What's more likely?
options: She might be looking around the room at everyone.
She definitely hates me.
I should just look down and hide.

1.tip: Reframe: You can't actually read minds! Ask yourself, 'What's the evidence?' Usually there's none.

2.definition: Deciding you know what people are thinking, then treating that guess like a fact.
2.scenarioDoneTo: You post a photo and only get 3 likes. You think, 'Everyone must think it's stupid.'
2.scenarioYouDo: You post a photo and only get 3 likes. You think, 'Everyone must think it's stupid.'

challenge.scenario: Your post only gets 3 likes and you think, 'Everyone hates it.' What's a more honest reframe?
options: 'Most people probably didn't even see it. Likes aren't a mind-reading device.'
'They all secretly hate it.'
'I should delete it right now.'

2.tip: Reframe: 'What proof do I actually have?' If someone hasn't said it, you're guessing.

3.definition: Projecting your own fears onto others and treating those projections as truth. Costs you accuracy and often damages relationships.
3.scenarioDoneTo: A colleague was short with you in a meeting. You assume, 'She thinks my work is trash and wants me off the project.'
3.scenarioYouDo: A colleague was short with you in a meeting. You assume, 'She thinks my work is trash and wants me off the project.'

challenge.scenario: A colleague is short in a meeting and you decide she wants you off the project. What's a better move?
options: Ask her directly: 'Hey — wanted to check in, everything okay?'
Assume she hates my work and start withdrawing.
Complain about her to someone else.

3.tip: Reframe: The cure for mind reading is a real conversation. Ask, don't assume.

1.definition: Predicting the future — usually predicting it'll go badly — as if it's already true.
1.scenarioDoneTo: Before your school play, you think, 'I know I'm going to mess up my lines and everyone will laugh at me.'
1.scenarioYouDo: Before your school play, you think, 'I know I'm going to mess up my lines and everyone will laugh at me.'

challenge.scenario: You predict you'll mess up the play before it even happens. What's a healthier thought?
options: 'I've practiced. I don't actually know what will happen — I'll do my best.'
'I should just fake being sick.'
'I'll definitely mess up, so why try?'

1.tip: Reframe: 'I don't have a crystal ball.' The future isn't written yet.

2.definition: Being so sure something bad will happen that you don't even try — and then you can never find out you were wrong.
2.scenarioDoneTo: You want to ask someone to hang out, but you tell yourself, 'They'll definitely say no,' so you never ask.
2.scenarioYouDo: You want to ask someone to hang out, but you tell yourself, 'They'll definitely say no,' so you never ask.

challenge.scenario: You're sure they'll say no, so you don't ask. What's a better reframe?
options: 'I actually don't know what they'll say. The only way to find out is to ask.'
'They'd say no, so it's not worth asking.'
'I'll wait for them to ask me instead — forever.'

2.tip: Reframe: When you assume the answer, you never get the real one. Test the prediction.

3.definition: Confusing a fear with a forecast. Your brain treats 'this could go badly' as 'this will go badly' and behavior follows the prediction.
3.scenarioDoneTo: You skip applying to a job you'd love because 'they'll never hire me.'
3.scenarioYouDo: You skip applying to a job you'd love because 'they'll never hire me.'

challenge.scenario: You skip the application, sure you'd be rejected. What's the reframe?
options: 'Not applying guarantees I don't get it. Applying gives me a real chance.'
'They'd never pick me, so save the effort.'
'I'll wait until I'm 100% qualified' (which is never).'

3.tip: Reframe: Predicted rejection isn't real rejection. The only way to know is to try.

1.definition: Thinking something is your fault when it actually isn't. Sometimes stuff just happens — it's not about you.
1.scenarioDoneTo: Your mom seems grumpy this morning and you think, 'She's mad at me. I must have done something wrong.'
1.scenarioYouDo: Your mom seems grumpy this morning and you think, 'She's mad at me. I must have done something wrong.'

challenge.scenario: Mom is grumpy and you assume it's your fault. What's more likely?
options: She might be tired or stressed about something else — it may have nothing to do with me.
It's definitely all my fault.
I should hide until she cheers up.

1.tip: Reframe: Not everything is about you. People have their own days going on.

2.definition: Taking blame for things you didn't cause — including other people's moods and choices.
2.scenarioDoneTo: Your parents are arguing and you think, 'This is because of me. If I were a better kid, they wouldn't fight.'
2.scenarioYouDo: Your parents are arguing and you think, 'This is because of me. If I were a better kid, they wouldn't fight.'

challenge.scenario: You blame yourself for your parents' argument. What's a truer thought?
options: 'Adults have their own issues. Their argument is not my fault or my job to fix.'
'If I was better, they wouldn't fight.'
'I need to be the perfect kid so they stop.'

2.tip: Reframe: Other people's emotions belong to them. You didn't cause it, and you can't fix it.

3.definition: Assuming responsibility for outcomes that had many causes, most of them outside your control. It sounds humble but it's actually a distortion of scale.
3.scenarioDoneTo: Your team missed a quarterly target and you think, 'This is entirely my fault.'
3.scenarioYouDo: Your team missed a quarterly target and you think, 'This is entirely my fault.'

challenge.scenario: You take 100% of the blame for a team miss. What's the reframe?
options: 'What was my actual share? What was outside my control? Both matter.'
'Yeah, it's all on me.'
'I should quit.'

3.tip: Reframe: Own your part, not everyone's. Ask: 'What's mine, what's shared, what's not mine at all?'

1.definition: Telling yourself you 'should' be different than you are — which usually just makes you feel worse.
1.scenarioDoneTo: You forgot your homework and think, 'I should never forget things. I'm so stupid.'
1.scenarioYouDo: You forgot your homework and think, 'I should never forget things. I'm so stupid.'

challenge.scenario: You forgot homework and beat yourself up with 'shoulds.' What's kinder and more useful?
options: 'Everyone forgets things sometimes. Let me set a reminder for tomorrow.'
'I'm the worst, I should be perfect.'
'I'll just give up on school.'

1.tip: Reframe: Swap 'should' for 'I want to' or 'next time.' It's less punishing and more helpful.

2.definition: Living by strict internal rules ('I should always be nice,' 'I shouldn't feel anxious') that make normal being-a-human feel like failure.
2.scenarioDoneTo: You feel nervous before a party and think, 'I shouldn't feel this way. I should be more confident.'
2.scenarioYouDo: You feel nervous before a party and think, 'I shouldn't feel this way. I should be more confident.'

challenge.scenario: You judge yourself for feeling nervous. What's a healthier reframe?
options: 'Nervous is a normal feeling before something new. I can feel nervous and still go.'
'I should feel nothing.'
'I'll just skip the party.'

2.tip: Reframe: 'Should' rules are made up. Feelings aren't wrong — they're information.

3.definition: Internalized 'shoulds' inherited from culture, family, or old fears. Trading them for values-based choices ('I choose to' / 'it matters to me that') restores agency.
3.scenarioDoneTo: You skip going to therapy because 'I shouldn't need help. I should be able to handle this alone.'
3.scenarioYouDo: You skip going to therapy because 'I shouldn't need help. I should be able to handle this alone.'

challenge.scenario: 'I shouldn't need help' keeps you from therapy. What's the reframe?
options: 'Getting help is a skill, not a weakness. I choose to take care of my mental health.'
'Real adults handle everything alone.'
'I'll just push through.'

3.tip: Reframe: 'I choose to' beats 'I should' every time. Values > rules.

1.definition: Believing something is true just because you feel it. Feelings are real, but they're not always facts.
1.scenarioDoneTo: You feel stupid after getting an answer wrong in class, and decide, 'I really AM stupid.'
1.scenarioYouDo: You feel stupid after getting an answer wrong in class, and decide, 'I really AM stupid.'

challenge.scenario: You feel stupid, so you decide you ARE stupid. What's a truer thought?
options: 'Feeling something doesn't make it true. I got one answer wrong — that's not who I am.'
'The feeling is the fact.'
'I'll never raise my hand again.'

1.tip: Reframe: 'I feel it' ≠ 'It's true.' Feelings are weather, not the whole sky.

2.definition: Using emotions as proof. 'I feel like a loser, so I must be one.' Your mood is coloring your beliefs about yourself.
2.scenarioDoneTo: You feel lonely at lunch and think, 'I feel like no one likes me, so no one must like me.'
2.scenarioYouDo: You feel lonely at lunch and think, 'I feel like no one likes me, so no one must like me.'

challenge.scenario: Lonely feelings become 'nobody likes me.' What's a healthier reframe?
options: 'Feeling lonely right now doesn't mean I have no friends. Feelings shift.'
'The feeling is proof.'
'I should give up on friends.'

2.tip: Reframe: Emotions are signals, not verdicts. Check them against actual evidence.

3.definition: Treating emotional experience as objective data. It leads to identity claims ('I am unlovable,' 'I am a fraud') that survive despite contradicting evidence.
3.scenarioDoneTo: Despite consistent positive feedback, you feel like a fraud at work and conclude, 'I really am a fraud.'
3.scenarioYouDo: Despite consistent positive feedback, you feel like a fraud at work and conclude, 'I really am a fraud.'

challenge.scenario: Feeling like a fraud, you conclude you ARE one — despite good feedback. What's the reframe?
options: 'The feeling is real. That doesn't make it accurate. What does the evidence actually show?'
'My feelings know the truth.'
'I should quit before they figure it out.'

3.tip: Reframe: Impostor feelings are common in growth. Separate the feeling from the fact.

1.definition: Sticking a big label on yourself (or someone else) instead of just describing what happened.
1.scenarioDoneTo: You drop your lunch tray and think, 'I'm such a loser.'
1.scenarioYouDo: You drop your lunch tray and think, 'I'm such a loser.'

challenge.scenario: You drop a tray and call yourself a loser. What's a truer thought?
options: 'I dropped a tray. That's a thing that happened, not who I am.'
'I really am a loser.'
'I should be embarrassed forever.'

1.tip: Reframe: Describe the moment, not your whole self. 'I did X' ≠ 'I AM X.'

2.definition: Turning behaviors into identities. One mistake becomes 'I'm stupid,' one lie becomes 'I'm a liar,' one bad game becomes 'I suck.'
2.scenarioDoneTo: You blew a test question and think, 'I'm stupid,' instead of 'I missed that one.'
2.scenarioYouDo: You blew a test question and think, 'I'm stupid,' instead of 'I missed that one.'

challenge.scenario: One missed question becomes 'I'm stupid.' What's healthier?
options: 'I got that one wrong. I'll review it. That's different from being stupid.'
'Yep, stupid confirmed.'
'I'll never get anything right.'

2.tip: Reframe: Behavior is changeable. Identity feels permanent. Don't confuse them.

3.definition: Global self-labeling collapses complexity into a single word. It's efficient and inaccurate — humans are not one adjective.
3.scenarioDoneTo: A relationship ends and you decide, 'I'm just unlovable.'
3.scenarioYouDo: A relationship ends and you decide, 'I'm just unlovable.'

challenge.scenario: You label yourself 'unlovable' after a breakup. What's the reframe?
options: 'One relationship ended. That's data about fit, not proof about my worth.'
'Nobody could love me.'
'I'll be alone forever.'

3.tip: Reframe: No one word is you. Zoom in on specific behaviors and situations instead.

1.definition: Brushing off the good stuff. 'It doesn't count.' 'That was luck.' 'They're just being nice.'
1.scenarioDoneTo: You get an A on your project and think, 'It was probably an easy assignment. It doesn't really count.'
1.scenarioYouDo: You get an A on your project and think, 'It was probably an easy assignment. It doesn't really count.'

challenge.scenario: You dismiss your A. What's a healthier thought?
options: 'I worked hard and it paid off. I can let this win count.'
'It was easy so it doesn't matter.'
'Anyone could have done it.'

1.tip: Reframe: Let the good land. Wins count even when it's uncomfortable to say so.

2.definition: Explaining away positives ('they had to say that,' 'anyone could do that') so they can't build up your sense of self.
2.scenarioDoneTo: A friend compliments your art and you think, 'They're just saying that to be nice.'
2.scenarioYouDo: A friend compliments your art and you think, 'They're just saying that to be nice.'

challenge.scenario: You brush off a genuine compliment. What's the reframe?
options: 'Say thanks. Let it in. Compliments aren't lies just because they're kind.'
'They didn't mean it.'
'I should argue with them.'

2.tip: Reframe: 'Thank you' is a full sentence. You don't have to talk yourself out of good news.

3.definition: Systematic filter that only lets negatives in as evidence about you. Over time it starves your self-image.
3.scenarioDoneTo: After a promotion you think, 'They just needed to fill the role. It's not about my ability.'
3.scenarioYouDo: After a promotion you think, 'They just needed to fill the role. It's not about my ability.'

challenge.scenario: You dismiss your promotion as luck. What's the reframe?
options: 'Multiple people chose me over other candidates. That's evidence I earned it.'
'It was pure luck.'
'I don't deserve it.'

3.tip: Reframe: If you'd count it as evidence when someone else did it, count it when you do it.

1.definition: Focusing on one bad thing and ignoring everything good, like there's a filter over your brain.
1.scenarioDoneTo: You had a fun day, but one kid called you a name. Now you can only think about that one moment.
1.scenarioYouDo: You had a fun day, but one kid called you a name. Now you can only think about that one moment.

challenge.scenario: One mean comment ate the whole day. What's a truer picture?
options: 'A bunch of good stuff happened AND one bad thing. Both are real.'
'That one thing ruined everything.'
'The whole day was terrible.'

1.tip: Reframe: Widen the lens. Ask, 'What ELSE happened today?'

2.definition: Picking out the single negative detail in a long list and letting it define the whole experience.
2.scenarioDoneTo: You performed 9 songs well at recital and hit one wrong note. All you can think about is the wrong note.
2.scenarioYouDo: You performed 9 songs well at recital and hit one wrong note. All you can think about is the wrong note.

challenge.scenario: 9 good songs, 1 wrong note — you obsess over the note. What's healthier?
options: '9 out of 10 were great. One mistake doesn't erase the rest.'
'The whole recital was ruined.'
'I'll never perform again.'

2.tip: Reframe: Count the whole scoreboard, not just the miss.

3.definition: Selective attention to negative information. It's biologically old (threat detection) but chronic use warps your self-narrative.
3.scenarioDoneTo: You get a performance review with 20 positive notes and 2 development areas. You spiral on the 2.
3.scenarioYouDo: You get a performance review with 20 positive notes and 2 development areas. You spiral on the 2.

challenge.scenario: You spiral on 2 negatives in a 22-item review. What's the reframe?
options: 'Both the strengths and the growth areas are useful data. Neither cancels the other.'
'The 2 negatives are the real review.'
'The positives were just filler.'

3.tip: Reframe: Read the whole page. Growth areas are how you get better — not the verdict on you.

1.definition: Deciding that because something happened once, it will always happen. 'Always' and 'never' are giveaway words.
1.scenarioDoneTo: One kid says no to playing with you at recess. You think, 'Nobody EVER wants to play with me.'
1.scenarioYouDo: One kid says no to playing with you at recess. You think, 'Nobody EVER wants to play with me.'

challenge.scenario: One 'no' becomes 'nobody ever.' What's a truer thought?
options: 'One person said no today. That doesn't mean everyone always will.'
'Nobody will ever play with me.'
'I'll play alone forever.'

1.tip: Reframe: Catch the 'always' and 'never.' They're almost always wrong.

2.definition: Turning a single event into a lifelong pattern. One rejection becomes 'I always get rejected.'
2.scenarioDoneTo: One person you liked wasn't interested. You think, 'This ALWAYS happens to me. I'll NEVER find someone.'
2.scenarioYouDo: One person you liked wasn't interested. You think, 'This ALWAYS happens to me. I'll NEVER find someone.'

challenge.scenario: One rejection becomes 'always/never.' What's the reframe?
options: 'One person, one moment. That's a data point, not a life sentence.'
'Nobody will ever want me.'
'This is my whole story.'

2.tip: Reframe: A sample size of 1 isn't a pattern.

3.definition: Drawing sweeping conclusions from limited data. Efficient for survival, terrible for accurate self-knowledge.
3.scenarioDoneTo: One pitch didn't land and you decide, 'I'm bad at pitching. I always will be.'
3.scenarioYouDo: One pitch didn't land and you decide, 'I'm bad at pitching. I always will be.'

challenge.scenario: One failed pitch → 'I'll always be bad at this.' What's the reframe?
options: 'Specific pitch, specific audience, specific day. What can I learn for next time?'
'I'm just bad at this forever.'
'I should never pitch again.'

3.tip: Reframe: Trade 'always/never' for 'sometimes/this time.' It's more accurate and less demoralizing.

1.definition: Measuring yourself against other people and always coming up short. Comparison steals your joy.
1.scenarioDoneTo: Your classmate got picked for the lead in the play and you didn't. You think, 'They're better than me at everything.'
1.scenarioYouDo: Your classmate got picked for the lead in the play and you didn't. You think, 'They're better than me at everything.'

challenge.scenario: You decide they're better 'at everything.' What's a truer thought?
options: 'They're better at this ONE thing right now. I'm good at other things.'
'They win at everything, I lose at everything.'
'I should give up on plays.'

1.tip: Reframe: Compare your own before and after, not you vs. someone else's highlight reel.

2.definition: Constantly measuring yourself against curated versions of others — especially online. Everyone's posting their wins, not their struggles.
2.scenarioDoneTo: You scroll social media and everyone seems happier, prettier, and more successful than you.
2.scenarioYouDo: You scroll social media and everyone seems happier, prettier, and more successful than you.

challenge.scenario: Social media makes you feel like everyone's ahead. What's the reframe?
options: 'I'm comparing my behind-the-scenes to their highlight reel. That's not a fair fight.'
'They really are all better.'
'I should feel bad.'

2.tip: Reframe: Social feeds are edited. Nobody posts the boring or bad parts.

3.definition: Social comparison distorts because you compare full internal experience (your doubt, fear, effort) with only observable output of others.
3.scenarioDoneTo: A peer just launched a company and you think, 'I'm so far behind. What am I even doing?'
3.scenarioYouDo: A peer just launched a company and you think, 'I'm so far behind. What am I even doing?'

challenge.scenario: A peer's launch makes you feel behind. What's the reframe?
options: 'Different lanes, different timing. My path isn't slower — it's mine.'
'I really am behind at life.'
'I should just quit.'

3.tip: Reframe: Run your own race. Progress vs. yourself is the only fair comparison.

1.definition: Making small problems feel huge (magnifying) or making your strengths feel tiny (minimizing).
1.scenarioDoneTo: You forgot one word in your class presentation and think, 'That was the WORST thing ever. Everyone will remember it forever.'
1.scenarioYouDo: You forgot one word in your class presentation and think, 'That was the WORST thing ever. Everyone will remember it forever.'

challenge.scenario: One forgotten word becomes 'worst thing ever.' What's a truer thought?
options: 'It was awkward for a second. In a week no one will remember.'
'They'll remember this forever.'
'I can never present again.'

1.tip: Reframe: Ask, 'Will this matter in a week? A month? A year?' Usually the answer shrinks the problem.

2.definition: Zooming in on flaws with a microscope and looking at strengths through the wrong end of a telescope.
2.scenarioDoneTo: You aced 4 subjects and got a C in one. You focus 100% on the C.
2.scenarioYouDo: You aced 4 subjects and got a C in one. You focus 100% on the C.

challenge.scenario: You obsess over one C, ignoring 4 A's. What's the reframe?
options: '4 A's and 1 C is a great semester with one area to improve.'
'The C ruined the report card.'
'I'm bad at school.'

2.tip: Reframe: Use the same magnification for wins as for losses. Fair reporting.

3.definition: Distortion of proportion that skews self-assessment and decision-making. Real problems shrink, minor ones balloon.
3.scenarioDoneTo: You had a great quarter but one client complaint and you decide the whole quarter was a failure.
3.scenarioYouDo: You had a great quarter but one client complaint and you decide the whole quarter was a failure.

challenge.scenario: One complaint erases a great quarter in your mind. What's the reframe?
options: 'A great quarter plus one issue to address. Both are true.'
'The complaint is the whole story.'
'The quarter was a failure.'

3.tip: Reframe: Real perspective sizes things accurately. Big things big, small things small.

1.definition: Blaming someone else for how you feel, or blaming yourself for everything. Real life is usually a mix.
1.scenarioDoneTo: You lost a game and yell, 'It's YOUR fault!' at your teammate.
1.scenarioYouDo: You lost a game and yell, 'It's YOUR fault!' at your teammate.

challenge.scenario: You blame your teammate for the loss. What's a healthier response?
options: 'We lost as a team. Let's figure out what we can do better together.'
'It's all their fault.'
'I'm never playing with them again.'

1.tip: Reframe: Look for shared responsibility. Blame ends teams; problem-solving builds them.

2.definition: Locating 100% of the cause outside yourself (or 100% inside). Both extremes distort what actually happened.
2.scenarioDoneTo: You bombed a chemistry test and think, 'My teacher is TERRIBLE. This is entirely her fault.'
2.scenarioYouDo: You bombed a chemistry test and think, 'My teacher is TERRIBLE. This is entirely her fault.'

challenge.scenario: You blame the teacher 100% for the bad test. What's more accurate?
options: 'The teaching may not be great AND I didn't prep enough. Both are real. I control the second one.'
'She's entirely to blame.'
'Nothing I do would help.'

2.tip: Reframe: Ask, 'What's my share? What's theirs? What's the situation?' Then act on your share.

3.definition: Attribution distortion. Externalizing blocks growth; over-internalizing crushes self-worth. Balanced attribution is a core resilience skill.
3.scenarioDoneTo: A project fails and you either blame the whole team or take 100% of the fault. Neither is fully true.
3.scenarioYouDo: A project fails and you either blame the whole team or take 100% of the fault. Neither is fully true.

challenge.scenario: You swing between 'all them' or 'all me' after a project fail. What's the reframe?
options: 'Multiple factors. My part, their part, the context. All useful data for next time.'
'Pure blame on someone.'
'Pure blame on me.'

3.tip: Reframe: Balanced attribution = 'What was mine, what was shared, what was outside anyone's control?'

1.definition: Getting stuck on 'it's not fair!' even when nothing can be done about it. Fair and unfair are real — but sitting in unfairness doesn't fix it.
1.scenarioDoneTo: Your sibling got a bigger piece of cake. You think, 'That's not fair! I hate this!'
1.scenarioYouDo: Your sibling got a bigger piece of cake. You think, 'That's not fair! I hate this!'

challenge.scenario: The cake wasn't fair. What's a helpful next move?
options: 'I can mention it calmly, or let it go and enjoy my slice.'
'Ruin dessert for everyone.'
'Stay mad forever.'

1.tip: Reframe: Fair matters. Getting stuck on unfair matters less. Notice it, act if you can, move on if you can't.

2.definition: Ruminating on unfairness turns temporary frustration into lasting resentment. Fair is a value, not a guarantee.
2.scenarioDoneTo: You worked harder on a group project but everyone got the same grade. You stay furious for weeks.
2.scenarioYouDo: You worked harder on a group project but everyone got the same grade. You stay furious for weeks.

challenge.scenario: The unfair grade eats at you for weeks. What's the reframe?
options: 'It was unfair. I can name it, learn from it, and stop letting it own my week.'
'I'll be mad forever.'
'I'll refuse to do group work ever.'

2.tip: Reframe: Naming unfairness is fine. Living in it hurts you more than anyone else.

3.definition: Fairness demands become identity when unaddressed. Distinguish 'this was unfair' (accurate) from 'the world owes me fairness' (a setup for chronic resentment).
3.scenarioDoneTo: A colleague got promoted before you despite you doing more. Months later you're still bitter.
3.scenarioYouDo: A colleague got promoted before you despite you doing more. Months later you're still bitter.

challenge.scenario: You're still bitter about an unfair promotion. What's the reframe?
options: 'It was unfair. Now what's the best move for MY next chapter?'
'Stay resentful and hope karma hits.'
'Nothing will ever be fair.'

3.tip: Reframe: 'It was unfair' can be true AND you can still choose your next move.

1.definition: Deciding you know what's happening without checking. Your brain fills in the blanks with the scariest guess.
1.scenarioDoneTo: Your parent asks 'Can we talk?' and you immediately think, 'I'm in HUGE trouble!'
1.scenarioYouDo: Your parent asks 'Can we talk?' and you immediately think, 'I'm in HUGE trouble!'

challenge.scenario: 'Can we talk?' → huge trouble in your head. What's a healthier thought?
options: 'Could be a hundred things. I'll find out when we actually talk.'
'Prepare for the worst.'
'Hide until they forget.'

1.tip: Reframe: Wait for actual information before deciding what's happening.

2.definition: Combining Mind Reading and Fortune Telling: assuming both what people think AND how it will end. Double the guessing.
2.scenarioDoneTo: Your crush hasn't texted back in 20 minutes. You conclude they're ghosting you forever.
2.scenarioYouDo: Your crush hasn't texted back in 20 minutes. You conclude they're ghosting you forever.

challenge.scenario: 20 minutes of silence becomes 'ghosted forever.' What's a truer thought?
options: 'People are busy. 20 minutes is nothing. I don't have to write the ending yet.'
'Definitely ghosted.'
'I'll never text again.'

2.tip: Reframe: Data before drama. Wait for evidence before writing the story.

3.definition: Pattern-completion under uncertainty. Your brain hates blanks and fills them fast — usually with the emotionally loudest guess, not the most accurate.
3.scenarioDoneTo: An email from HR marked 'sensitive' triggers you to assume you're being fired.
3.scenarioYouDo: An email from HR marked 'sensitive' triggers you to assume you're being fired.

challenge.scenario: HR email = 'I'm being fired.' What's the reframe?
options: 'HR emails cover a lot of topics. I'll read it before I panic.'
'Update the resume immediately.'
'Confront my manager preemptively.'

3.tip: Reframe: Open the email. Fear guesses way worse than reality most of the time.

1.definition: Thinking you have to control everything — or thinking you can't control anything. Real life is a mix of both.
1.scenarioDoneTo: It rained on your birthday and you feel like YOU ruined it somehow.
1.scenarioYouDo: It rained on your birthday and you feel like YOU ruined it somehow.

challenge.scenario: You feel like the rain is your fault. What's a truer thought?
options: 'Weather is not something I control. I can still make the day fun indoors.'
'I ruined it.'
'Nothing good ever happens.'

1.tip: Reframe: Separate 'things I control' from 'things I don't.' Focus on the first list.

2.definition: Believing you must manage everyone's feelings, or that you have no influence at all. Both flavors are exhausting.
2.scenarioDoneTo: You feel responsible for making sure your friend group is always happy.
2.scenarioYouDo: You feel responsible for making sure your friend group is always happy.

challenge.scenario: You feel like everyone's mood is your job. What's healthier?
options: 'I influence the vibe. I don't control everyone's feelings. That's not my job.'
'It's all on me.'
'I need to make everyone happy always.'

2.tip: Reframe: You are one person in a group. Own your part, not everyone else's.

3.definition: Distortion of agency. Over-control drives burnout and controlling behavior; under-control drives helplessness. The sweet spot is calibrated influence.
3.scenarioDoneTo: You micromanage every part of a project because if you don't, 'nothing will get done right.'
3.scenarioYouDo: You micromanage every part of a project because if you don't, 'nothing will get done right.'

challenge.scenario: You micromanage because you can't trust it to others. What's the reframe?
options: 'What can I delegate and coach vs. own directly? I don't have to hold everything.'
'Only I can do it right.'
'Give up and disengage.'

3.tip: Reframe: Calibrated control > total control. Trust + verify beats grip-of-death every time.
